title: Genuine question about AI-assisted game dev: Why is the pushback so strong when a human is still driving the project?
author: WideWealth7349
selftext:
I've been working on a game for the past 4 weeks using Claude to help with parts of the code. Recently I shared a clip looking for constructive feedback to improve and most of the reaction was just instant dismissal because AI was involved rather than actual feedback on the gameplay.  
I completely understand why low effort AI asset flips get criticized. At the same time you obviously can't just prompt make me a game and publish it. You still have to understand architecture, fix bugs, balance systems and connect everything so the game actually feels coherent and has soul. That still depends 100% on the person behind the project.  
With major studios integrating AI into their tooling right now it feels like the role of a system integrator who holds the vision and brings the pieces together is becoming just as important as writing every line of code manually.  
For those who are strongly against AI tools in indie dev I'd genuinely like to understand the core issue from your perspective. Is it mainly concern about job displacement and years of learned skills being automated or is it more about quality and copyright concerns?

At the end of the day most players just care if a game is fun and runs well. I hope this post works better for a real discussion. I'm not trying to put anyone down here I just want a calm honest conversation about using AI in game dev. Let's keep this respectful and constructive so we can actually have a good discussion

comments.author: SquirrelinaboxMedia
comments.body:
Just like some people blanket all AI assisted products as "AI slop" you are kind of clumping all people that have any kind of problem with AI as "anti AI".   The reality is that while some are against any ai whatsoever, many have specific issues with certain aspects.

For instance, with games it seems like what most are against is AI use replacing the artistic aspects of the game (graphics, sounds, music, voices, etc).  The issue there is sure, you are "directing" the AI to come up with a certain song or voice but the actual work being done there is the AI that was trained on real artists.

Then on top of that even AI for just being a tool to assist with coding and other aspects still means that AI is doing the work that humans used to, which means fewer jobs.  That same issue came up with industrialization and automation and various other big advancements through history.  

With that all being said, for me personally, I wish AI had never advanced to where it has now.  I think it will do more harm than good.  But the reality is that it is here and I am using it for a variety of projects because I can't put that genie back into the bottle myself, so I may as well start making wishes.

comments.author: KevinDL
comments.body:
I work in developer relations at Bezi, so I talk with game developers about AI pretty much every day. Professionally, the reaction I see is a lot more mixed than it can look in a Reddit thread. I know developers who love these tools because they make parts of their job easier, developers who are wary of what adoption means for their jobs, and plenty who feel both ways. A good chunk of the people I talk to are actively learning how to use them because they want to stay competitive when they apply for their next role.

I think knowing how to work with AI is already becoming a hiring advantage in some roles, and I expect it to become an expectation in more of them over the next few years. Professional workflows change, and choosing to sit out a change can narrow your options. I understand why that makes people uneasy, especially when they’ve spent years getting good at their craft and have little say in how their employer rolls out these tools.

On the indie side, a lot of the loudest takes I see online come from people reacting to games from the outside. Among developers I talk to, some of the strongest reservations come from artists, especially around whether their work was used to train models with their consent. Questions about consent and copyright, environmental costs, and what this means for people’s livelihoods all deserve a real discussion.

The part I’d push on is what it means for a human to be driving the project. From what you described, you’re making the design decisions and using Claude to help with parts of the code. You’re still figuring out how the systems fit together, fixing bugs, balancing the game, and deciding whether it feels good to play. Some people hand over most creative decisions and ship whatever comes back, with very little iteration. I think that second kind of project has done a lot to shape what people picture when they hear “AI-assisted game.”

It reminds me of the early Unity days. You could watch a clip and think, “Yep, that’s a Unity game.” Enough rough releases had a similar look that being able to spot the engine became a knock against the game. Plenty of good games were being made in Unity the whole time. You just watched those clips and thought about the game.

I catch myself doing a version of that with AI today, even though I work in the space. If the art, animation, or UI has a generated look and the pieces feel like they belong to different games, I lose interest pretty quickly. Sometimes I give one a shot, and it turns out to be decent. But my first impression is already about how it was made. When a developer uses Claude or Bezi to get a mechanic working, I’m usually just thinking about whether that mechanic is fun.

replies.author: WideWealth7349
replies.body:
First of all, thank you so much for taking the time to write such a detailed answer, especially coming straight from someone who talks to developers every day.

I get the concerns around consent and artists' work, and I don't think they should be brushed aside.

For me the human part is basically everything about the game itself. I decide what goes in, how the systems fit together, how it's balanced and whether it feels good to play. I've played MMOs since I was a kid, so I'm building the one I wish still existed, with that early 2000s feel.

My workflow is pretty hands-on. I break features into small steps and let Claude help with the code. Then I look at what changed, test it myself in the game, and usually go through a few rounds of changes until it feels right. I use version control so I can see exactly what changed and roll back if something goes wrong, and I run frontend and backend tests and build checks before anything goes live. But nothing replaces actually playing it.

I also have my own asset pipeline built from several tools, and a big reason for that is exactly what you describe. I don't want it to look like typical AI output, where everything feels like it comes from a different game. So I put a lot of effort into getting a consistent style, and I check and adjust the results before they go into the game. Your Unity comparison is spot on. I'd like the game to be judged as a game, not by that AI look

replies.author: WideWealth7349
replies.body:
Honestly, this is the kind of criticism I actually find helpful because you’re pointing out specific things instead of just calling the project AI slop.  
I agree with you on the skills. I’ve actually noticed myself that there are way too many at the moment, and that’s something I need to go back to and rethink properly. I don’t want a huge list of abilities just for the sake of having a huge list. They need to make sense, feel different from each other, fit the classes and progression, and actually be fun to use. That’s definitely something I need to work on.  
I also agree that the visuals aren’t consistent yet. Some assets don’t fit together properly, and there’s still a lot of work to do on the art direction. The screenshots weren’t uploaded in the original quality either, so I’d honestly recommend looking at the game directly in the browser.

But I think it’s also important to put things into perspective. I’ve been working on this for about four weeks. I never said it was finished, ready for release, or anywhere near a fully developed MMORPG. I was just sharing an early look at what I’d been working on.

And honestly, those four weeks weren’t even four full weeks of regular development. It was roughly four really intensive sessions. I was basically pushing things as far as I could during those sessions, so obviously there’s a lot that still needs to be revisited, refined, and properly developed. There’s also a lot more going on behind the scenes than what you can see in a screenshot. I’m working on the architecture, networking, security, privacy, performance, memory management, the asset pipeline, gameplay systems and a lot of other things that need to work properly for a game like this.  
And just to clarify something about the assets: apart from the character models, everything else so far has been developed through my own pipeline. The icons, buttons, UI elements, textures and all the other graphical elements are my own work. I’m not saying they’re perfect, because they clearly still need work, but they’re not just random assets thrown together either. I have a pipeline behind them, and I intend to improve and refine everything as the project develops.

I’m using AI as a tool to help me develop the game, but that doesn’t mean Claude makes every decision and I just accept whatever it gives me. I have a vision for what I want Aether Online to become, and there’s a lot of planning, testing, changing and reworking involved.  
I know the game doesn’t look or feel like a finished MMORPG right now. That’s not the point. It’s a foundation, and I think it’s a pretty decent one considering how little time I’ve actually spent on it so far.

I’m not expecting everyone to like it, and I’m absolutely aware there’s a huge amount of work ahead. I just think there’s a difference between pointing out things that genuinely need improvement and judging a project as if it was supposed to be finished after a month. I’m happy to take criticism, especially when it’s constructive. I know the skills need work, the visuals need consistency, and the gameplay needs to develop much further. That’s part of building a game.

19 000 hours of listening to heavy metal doesnt mean you can compose a heavy metal song  
19 000 hours of reading novels doesnt mean you can write.

replies.author: CubersumGame
replies.body:
I fear that a blood-red veil of hatred toward AI has clouded your vision, leading you to intentionally muddle your own arguments.

For instance, you conflate mechanical skills - such as playing basketball - with intellectual skills, like reading and writing.

It is well-established - and confirmed by the experience of generations - that extensive reading fosters what is often called "innate literacy." This occurs simply because the brain learns to recognize correctly spelled words and internalizes natural, literary turns of phrase. This process enriches one’s vocabulary, and, eventually, someone who has read a great deal can indeed produce high-quality writing of their own.

The same principle applies to films or games. People who have watched many movies often become adept at anticipating plot twists; furthermore, if we look at YouTube reviewers, we find that their scripted, theatrical presentations are frequently very well-structured - a direct result of their accumulated experience in watching narratives for video. The same holds true for games.

Admittedly, there are poor examples. People might read books only to produce abysmal fan fiction, or create cringeworthy videos. But, as a rule, this usually stems from a lack of genuine exposure - the individual hasn't actually consumed enough books or films, but has instead decided to create something simply because they think it’s "cool" or for some similar, superficial reason.

In contrast, mechanical skills - such as playing basketball, touch-typing, or speaking a foreign language - truly require long, dedicated practice. This is precisely why a person might have a strong grasp of a foreign language (having read or listened to it extensively) yet still struggle to speak it. It is also the reason why there are distinct assessment scales for language comprehension versus speaking ability. If we take this distinction into account, it becomes clear that AI, as a "flawed tool," will only produce "flawed results" when used by people who lack sufficient reading or playing experience. In the same vein, the proliferation of computers has meant that any child can now type up and publish their own illiterate fan fiction - yet, at the same time, we have also seen a great deal of highly talented fan fiction emerge. Were these pieces written by professional authors? Far from always.

comments.author: HandStuckInToaster

Because there is genuinely a difference between the time and effort that goes into something, for some players that difference is what really matters to them. If i spend 30 hours of my human time 3D Modelling assets based on the skills, technique and style I've developed over years of 3D modelling assets it obviously has a perceived level of value higher than compared to me having an MCP tool a python asset in 3 minutes. 

Your right; some players entirely only care about if the game is good, others will only care about if it runs well, others will definitely  care about if they feel their money/time is being well spent and if they're feeling ripped off by purchasing something with little human creation apart from prompt oversight.

comments.author: Squishy_Red_Potato
comments.body:
I've talked with AI "Artists" who claim they put just as much work into creating a piece through AI, as a more traditional artist would have done drawing/paining/modeling by hand. Or developers who don't have any art skills and "don't have the money to hire someone" so they use genAI to make their assets.

Same goes for narrative, audio, animation and so on. Even design some times.

Ultimately the problem usually comes to a head because the person using genAI to build assets and large chunks of their game (or the entire game) don't actually understand the fundamentals of the things they're asking the tool to create. Especially with art, these tools are very good at creating things that on the surface look quite nice. But if you dig even a little bit into what was made with someone who understands the craft, you realize that it doesn't stand up to much scrutiny. You get things that appear technically correct on the surface, but for some reason never feels coherent or properly fun when experienced in-game.

I mean on paper the design makes sense! Why doesn't it feel fun? That's a lack of understanding of the craft of game design.

The concept art looks so cool! The character models are detailed! The environments have lots of stuff! Why doesn't it feel visually cohesive/why can't I figure out what I should be doing next. That's a lack of understanding of how to visually construct a world/scene that a player can navigate and understand.

It wrote lots of code and it does all kinds of complex things! But perf is bad, or multiplayer is glitchy. That's a lack of understanding of the engineering that goes into building a game.

These tools are very very good at building prototypes quickly. But to take it further to make an actual shipping game that's fun actually requires some of the deep technical skills that many here are using genAI to try and get out of learning.
